strengths: Addresses a useful computer vision problem: semantic segmentation without user-provided class names. Combining automatic vocabulary discovery with a pretrained segmentor offers a practical approach requiring no additional model training.

BCC provides a plausible technical contribution by feeding clustered subsets of BLIP patch embeddings into its native text decoder. This enables local descriptions that can capture objects missed by global captioning.

Experiments cover three diverse benchmarks. Table 1 provides encouraging evidence for local captioning: Self-Seg improves class-agnostic IoU over BLIP plus X-Decoder from 38.0 to 41.9 on VOC, 26.7 to 29.2 on ADE20K, and 29.2 to 35.8 on Cityscapes.

The pipeline is clearly illustrated, principal pretrained models and datasets are credited, and many implementation parameters are supplied. Appendix B usefully documents hallucinated classes, competing semantic labels, and overly generic descriptions.
weaknesses: The main evaluation component, LOVE, is insufficiently validated (Section 3.4 and Appendix A). Its prompts instruct the LLM to map stuff categories to background even for Cityscapes and ADE20K, which annotate such categories. ADE20K mapping additionally relies on the LLM recalling the taxonomy without receiving the actual 847-class vocabulary. Exact-name overrides do not resolve errors for non-exact category names. No human-audited mapping accuracy, prompt sensitivity analysis, or quantitative comparison with previous mappers is provided. Consequently, the reliability of the reported semantic mIoU remains uncertain.

The headline comparison with ZeroSeg is not demonstrably controlled. Table 2 reports 41.6 versus 20.1 on VOC without establishing that both methods use the same label-mapping evaluator. Self-Seg also relies on a pretrained X-Decoder segmentor, whereas the cited ZeroSeg work targets zero segment labels; these supervision regimes need explicit differentiation. No competing automatic-class baseline is reported on ADE20K or Cityscapes, limiting support for the state-of-the-art claims.

The ablations do not adequately isolate the contribution to semantic class discovery. Table 1 measures class-agnostic overlap, which cannot establish whether generated labels are correct. The straightforward BLIP plus X-Decoder baseline should also be evaluated using semantic mIoU under the same mapper and a matched captioning budget. Multiscale clustering, cross-cluster alignment, and denoising receive no component ablations, and the claimed applicability across segmentors is demonstrated only with X-Decoder.

Model selection is insufficiently specified. Section 4.1 describes Bayesian optimization against VOC mIoU without identifying an independent tuning split, while Table 2 uses the best dataset-specific captioning-cycle counts from Table 3. Clarifying the separation between tuning and reporting is necessary to assess possible selection optimism. Repeated runs are also needed to characterize variability from stochastic caption generation and clustering.

Several correctable implementation ambiguities impede reproducibility. Section 3.1 describes Hungarian matching, but Equation 10 specifies independent maximum-IoU assignments, which implement a different correspondence rule. Alignment between the 24-by-24 and 32-by-32 patch grids is underspecified, as is the handling of concatenated positional features before feeding the frozen BLIP decoder.

Practical computational cost is unquantified. The preferred Cityscapes configuration requires 20 captioning cycles, but the manuscript reports no inference latency, memory consumption, or accuracy-versus-runtime analysis. This limits assessment of the framework's practical impact.
